title: Harmonic Number Divisibility: Problem Overview
content: Erdős Problem #291 asks about the GCD structure of harmonic numbers. Writing $H_n = 1 + 1/2 + \cdots + 1/n = a_n/L_n$ where $L_n = \text{lcm}(1, \ldots, n)$, the question is: do both $\gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1$ and $\gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1$ occur infinitely often? Part 2 ($\gcd > 1$) is trivially YES via Wolstenholme's theorem; Part 1 ($\gcd = 1$) remains OPEN, connected to Schanuel's conjecture in transcendence theory.
mathContext: $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{k} = \frac{a_n}{L_n}$ where $L_n = \text{lcm}(1, \ldots, n)$. Key criterion: $p \mid \gcd(a_n, L_n) \iff p \mid \text{num}(H_k)$ where $k$ is the leading base-$p$ digit of $n$. Wolstenholme: $p^2 \mid \text{num}(H_{p-1})$ for $p \ge 5$.

title: Core Definitions: L_n, H_n, a_n, and the GCD
content: Defines the fundamental objects. $L(n) = \text{lcm}(1, 2, \ldots, n)$ via iterated lcm over a Finset. $H(n) = \sum_{k=1}^n 1/k$ as a rational number. The numerator $a(n) = H_n \cdot L_n$ as a natural number (since $k \mid L_n$ for all $k \le n$, this product is always an integer). The key quantity $\text{harmonicGCD}(n) = \gcd(a_n, L_n)$.
mathContext: $L(n) = \text{lcm}(1, \ldots, n)$. $H(n) = \sum_{k=1}^n k^{-1} \in \mathbb{Q}$. $a(n) = H_n \cdot L_n \in \mathbb{Z}$ (since each $k^{-1} \cdot L_n \in \mathbb{Z}$). $\text{harmonicGCD}(n) = \gcd(a_n, L_n)$.

title: The Problem Statement: Two Infinitude Questions
content: Formalizes both parts of Problem #291. `question_part1`: the set $\{n : \gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1\}$ is infinite. `question_part2`: the set $\{n : \gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1\}$ is infinite. The full conjecture `erdos291Statement` is their conjunction. Part 2 is proved in this formalization; Part 1 remains open.
mathContext: $\text{question\_part1}: |\{n : \gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1\}| = \infty$. $\text{question\_part2}: |\{n : \gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1\}| = \infty$. The full problem asks for both.

title: Steinerberger's Criterion and Wolstenholme's Theorem
content: The key theorem `steinerberger_criterion`: if the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$ equals $p - 1$, then $p \mid \gcd(a_n, L_n)$. This is actually proved (not axiomatized!) from two ingredients: the `divisibility_characterization` (relating divisibility to numerators of partial harmonic sums) and Wolstenholme's theorem ($p^2 \mid \text{num}(H_{p-1})$ for $p \ge 5$). The case $p = 3$ is handled by direct computation: $H_2 \cdot 2! = 3$, divisible by 3.
mathContext: Wolstenholme (1862): $p^2 \mid \text{num}(H_{p-1})$ for prime $p \ge 5$. Characterization: $p \mid \gcd(a_n, L_n) \iff p \mid \text{num}(H_k \cdot k!)$ where $k = $ leading digit of $n$ in base $p$. Combined: leading digit $p-1 \Rightarrow p \mid \gcd$.

title: Heuristic Analysis and Why Part 1 is Hard
content: Shiu (2016) gave a heuristic argument that $\#\{n \le x : \gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1\} \sim x/\log x$, suggesting Part 1 is true but with density 0. The idea: for $\gcd = 1$, we need $n$'s leading digit in base $p$ to avoid giving $p \mid \gcd$ for every prime $p \le n$. Since these conditions are 'almost independent' across primes, the probability is $\prod_p (1 - 1/p) \sim 1/\log n$ by Mertens' theorem. Wu-Yan (2022) proved conditionally (on Schanuel's conjecture) that the density of $\gcd > 1$ is 1.
mathContext: Heuristic: $\Pr[\gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1] \approx \prod_{p \le n} (1 - \Pr[p \mid \gcd]) \sim \prod_{p \le n} (1 - 1/p) \sim 2e^{-\gamma}/\log n$ by Mertens. Wu-Yan: assuming $\{1/\log p : p \text{ prime}\}$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent (from Schanuel), density of $\gcd > 1$ is 1.

title: Structural Properties of L_n and H_n
content: Proves foundational properties. For $L_n$: computed values $L(0)=1, L(1)=1, L(2)=2, \ldots, L(6)=60$; positivity $L(n) > 0$; divisibility $L(n) \mid n!$; and $k \mid L(n)$ for $1 \le k \le n$. For $H_n$: computed values $H(1)=1, H(2)=3/2, \ldots, H(6)=49/20$; recurrence $H(n+1) = H(n) + 1/(n+1)$; positivity; strict monotonicity; and monotonicity. Also proves $H_n \cdot L_n \ge 0$ and $H_n \cdot L_n = \sum_{k=1}^n L_n/k$.
mathContext: $L(n) \mid n!$ (since each $k \le n$ divides both $L(n)$ and $n!$). $H(n+1) = H(n) + \frac{1}{n+1}$. $H_n \cdot L_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{L_n}{k} \in \mathbb{Z}$. Computed: $L(6) = 60$, $H(6) = 49/20$.

title: Computed GCD Values: First Occurrence at n=6
content: Proves exact GCD values by computation. $\gcd(a_n, L_n) = 1$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $\gcd = 3$ at $n = 6$ (the first occurrence of $\gcd > 1$). Extended examples: $\gcd = 3$ for $n = 7, 8$ (all have leading digit 2 in base 3) and $\gcd = 1$ for $n = 9, 10$. Total: 7 values with $\gcd = 1$ found among $n \le 10$.

title: Leading Digit Theory and Infinite Families
content: Develops the theory of leading digits in base $p$. The key structural result `leadingDigit_pm1_times_pow`: for any $p > 1$ and $k \ge 0$, $\text{ld}((p-1) \cdot p^k, p) = p - 1$, because $(p-1) \cdot p^k$ in base $p$ is the digit $p-1$ followed by $k$ zeros. Combined with Steinerberger: $p \mid \gcd(a_{(p-1)p^k}, L_{(p-1)p^k})$ for any prime $p \ge 3$. This gives infinite families for $p = 3$ ($\{2 \cdot 3^k\}$) and $p = 5$ ($\{4 \cdot 5^k\}$).
mathContext: $(p-1) \cdot p^k$ in base $p$: $\underbrace{(p-1)}_{\text{leading}} \underbrace{00\ldots0}_{k \text{ zeros}}$. General theorem: $p \mid \gcd(a_{(p-1)p^k}, L_{(p-1)p^k})$ for prime $p \ge 3$, $k \ge 1$.

title: Part 2 Proved: Infinitely Many n with gcd > 1
content: The theorem `part2_trivially_true` proves Part 2 using the infinite family $\{2 \cdot 3^k : k \ge 1\}$. For each such $n$, $\text{ld}(n, 3) = 2 = 3 - 1$, so $3 \mid \gcd(a_n, L_n)$ by Steinerberger. An alternate proof `part2_via_five` uses $\{4 \cdot 5^k\}$. The summary theorem `erdos_291` packages Part 2 as the proved component.
mathContext: $\{2 \cdot 3^k : k \ge 1\} \subseteq \{n : \gcd(a_n, L_n) > 1\}$ is infinite. Proof: $k \mapsto 2 \cdot 3^{k+1}$ is injective and $3 \mid \gcd$ at each point. Similarly $\{4 \cdot 5^k\}$ provides a second family with $5 \mid \gcd$.

title: ZMod Computations and Concrete Evidence for Part 1
content: Computations in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ verify that $\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k^{-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ for $p = 3, 5, 7, 11, 13$. This is a consequence of the bijection $k \mapsto k^{-1}$ on $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*$ and the sum $\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k = p(p-1)/2 \equiv 0$ for odd $p$. The theorem `seven_gcd_one_values` assembles 7 concrete values ($n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10$) where $\gcd = 1$, providing computational evidence for Part 1.
mathContext: In $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$: $\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k^{-1} = \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k = \frac{p(p-1)}{2} \equiv 0$ for odd $p$. This is related to but weaker than Wolstenholme ($p^2$ divisibility requires deeper analysis). Evidence: 7 values with $\gcd = 1$ in $[1, 10]$.
